text:
The farmers market started like the tide. First it was nothing, then it crept up and then it just arrived and it was full. By seven the square was completely filled with the white tents and they were snapping in the wind, and their shadows were stretched out long and blue across the bricks. I came early, I always come early, with my folding table under one arm and a crate of tomatoes under the other. The tomatoes are not perfect. Some of them are split at the shoulder. Some have black freckles on them. But they smell of sun and dust. And I put them out in a nice pyramid, like jewels.
Across the aisle there's a woman called June, she does honey, and it's in jars that are the colour of late afternoon, and she waves at me. I'm wearing gloves, so I wave back. She says, you're late, the early birds bought the basil. And I say, let them, I'm here for the quiet. But the quiet never really lasts. The market starts to fill with noise. There's a guitar being played and there's a coffee urn hissing, and there's the clack of a knife on a chopping board. There's a little girl in yellow boots who has her nose pressed up to the glass where June's honey display is. There's a man in a linen apron who's arguing gently with a customer over the price of chard. And the air smells of wet earth, cinnamon, frying onion, and the sweet animal breath of peaches. And I stand behind my tomatoes and I look over my little red kingdom, and I feel like the keeper of this small world.
I've been coming to this market for thirty years. At first I came with my wife, Lena. She'd always buy flowers, even when we didn't have money for bread. Now I come alone. But my mind is a strange thing. It still expects to see her at the corner, with her head tilted to one side like a bird, listening to the rain, or listening to the stems of the sunflowers. It keeps the furniture in the same place, even when no one has been in there for a long time.
A boy comes up to my table. He's about nine. He's got a cowlick in his hair. Very serious. He's holding a five-dollar bill in his fist, like a flag. He says, are these yours? I say, yes. And he says, they're ugly. And I laugh. I say, they are. But they taste like the ones your grandmother used to grow. And he thinks about this. And he says, my grandmother doesn't grow tomatoes, she grows roses. And I say, well, then she'd know, roses and tomatoes both need patience. And he buys two tomatoes and carries them off, like they're eggs. I watch him go until he disappears into the crowd. And then the wind changes, and I smell rain from the west. And everyone starts looking at the sky. June covers her honey jars with a cloth. The guitar player sings a song about a river that runs on, even when nobody's watching.
By noon the market is thinning. I've sold almost everything. I'm packing my empty crate, folding my table. And I stand there for a moment. And I watch the tents flapping, like tired wings. And I see a woman buy the last of June's honey. And June smiles. And it's not a smile for the sale. It's a smile for the day, for making it through. And I walk past the flower stall. And there's a bucket of sunflowers on the edge of the pavement. And they're all turned towards the vanishing sun. And I stop. I haven't bought flowers in years. I felt it was a betrayal or a waste, or both. But there's the girl in the yellow boots again. She's holding a stem. And her mother is laughing at something the florist says. And it's bright and ordinary. And I remember Lena saying, markets are just kitchens with no walls. Everyone trading hunger and hope in the same open air. I didn't believe it then. I do now.
So I reach in my pocket. I buy a sunflower. I don't know why. And I walk home. The streets smell of rain. And the flower nods against my shoulder, like a small forgiving head. And I put it in a glass of water on my kitchen table. And I sit there and look at it for a long time. While the room grows dim. And the market, and Lena, and all the quiet Saturdays, settle around me, like a gentle, unasked-for grace.
